---
title: "Get started"
description: >
  From a data frame to a rendered plot: build a spec, layer marks, train
  scales, and render it into a vellum scene.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = requireNamespace("vellumplot", quietly = TRUE)
)
```

vellumplot is a declarative, pipe-first grammar of graphics built on the
[vellum](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellum/) backend. You describe a plot
as an inspectable, serializable *spec*; nothing is drawn until the spec is
compiled into a vellum scene and rendered.

## Install

vellumplot compiles a Rust crate (inside `vellum`), so you need a Rust toolchain
(`cargo`/`rustc`) on your machine alongside R. With that in place:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("r-vellum/vellumplot")
```

## A first plot

Start with `vplot()` on a data frame, then add a mark. Encodings (`x`, `y`,
`color`, …) are tidy-eval expressions evaluated against the data.

```{r}
library(vellumplot)

vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp) |>
  scale_color_continuous()
```

Printing a spec draws it into the plots pane (and embeds in a knitr/Quarto
chunk), like ggplot2.

## Layering marks

Add more marks to the same panel; scales train across every layer.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  mark_smooth(x = wt, y = mpg)
```

## Faceting

Split into a grid of panels with shared or free scales.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl)
```

## The spec is just data

Nothing is drawn until the spec is compiled. `summary()` shows its structure
without rendering.

```{r}
summary(vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp))
```

## Rendering to a file

`render_plot()` writes the compiled scene; the format follows the file
extension: `.png`, `.svg`, `.pdf` or `.pptx`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg)
render_plot(p, "cars.png")
```

The layout is solved once, by vellum, so the PNG, the SVG, the PDF and the
PowerPoint slide all share it.

### Saving to PowerPoint

A `.pptx` path writes a one-slide PowerPoint file of **editable shapes** at the
plot's size. Every point, bar and line is a DrawingML shape, every plain-text
label a text box you can retype (math and haloed labels are outlines), and each
panel a named group you can ungroup, recolour or move in PowerPoint. No other
package is needed.

```{r}
#| eval: false
render_plot(p, "cars.pptx")
```

`vellum::pptx_pages()` writes several plots as the slides of one deck, also
without officer:

```{r}
#| eval: false
p2 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 10)
vellum::pptx_pages(list(p, p2), "deck.pptx")
```

To put a plot on a slide of your own deck, built with
[officer](https://davidgohel.github.io/officer/), wrap it in `vellum::as_dml()`
and hand it to `officer::ph_with()`. The plot is laid out again at the size of
the placeholder, so its text keeps its point size and nothing is stretched
(`resize = FALSE` keeps the plot's own size).

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(officer)

deck <- read_pptx() |>
  add_slide(layout = "Title and Content") |>
  ph_with("Fuel economy", location = ph_location_type("title")) |>
  ph_with(vellum::as_dml(p), location = ph_location_type("body"))
print(deck, target = "fuel.pptx")
```

Fonts are named, not embedded: PowerPoint uses the font vellum measured the
text with when the machine opening the deck has it, and substitutes another
when it doesn't. `text = "outline"` (in `render_plot()`, `pptx_pages()` and
`as_dml()`) writes glyph outlines instead, which look the same everywhere but
can't be edited as text. DrawingML has no clipping, blend modes or masks, so
vellum cuts clipped geometry in advance and draws the parts it can't express
(a blur, a blend mode) as a picture, with a warning. PowerPoint output needs
vellum 0.18.0 or later; see vellum's
[`as_dml()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellum/reference/as_dml.html) and
[`pptx_pages()`](https://r-vellum.github.io/vellum/reference/pptx_pages.html)
for the details.

For many figures at once, `pdf_pages()` and `render_all()` are covered in
[Facets and composition](facets-and-composition.html#multi-page-and-batch-output).

### Strings and documents

`plot_svg()` returns the scene as an SVG string, and `plot_data_uri()` inlines a
plot as a self-contained `data:` URI (vector by default, or `format = "png"`) for
an `<img>`, a Markdown image, or an email — no separate file.

```{r}
#| eval: false
uri <- p |> plot_data_uri()          # data:image/svg+xml;base64,...
```

Inside a Quarto or R Markdown document you usually write nothing special: a
plot printed in a chunk adapts to the target — a crisp inline **SVG** for HTML
output, and the default vector/raster render for PDF or Word.
